requirements.note: Inset-grouped main screen: Today (22) and All (135), then 6 colour-coded lists, each with its open count. Counts update after completing, adding and deleting.
Open tasks come first, then a 'Completed (n)' header with a disclosure chevron that collapses and expands. Tapping a checkbox completes or reopens the task, and it moves between sections.

New Task sheet has a multiline title, notes, a Due Date switch that shows an inline graphical calendar, a None/Low/High segmented control and a List picker. Tapping a row opens a Details sheet; the edit saved.
Overdue dates are red with an exclamation icon and the word 'Overdue'. High priority shows a red !!!, low priority a grey !.
Swipe left shows a native Delete action. Reordering uses edit mode (List Options > Reorder Tasks) with system drag handles, and the new order persisted.
Add List button opens an alert with a text field. Rename works from the list's menu and from a swipe action. Swipe Delete asks for confirmation in an action sheet.
After relaunch: the renamed list, the new order, the edited and added task, the deletions and the completions all survived.

tells: The selected day in the inline calendar is a black filled circle instead of the accent-tinted selection.
Reordering is hidden behind List Options > Reorder Tasks instead of being available directly in the list.
At the largest text size the low-priority '!' hangs beside a wrapped title, so the title's second line is indented oddly.
A.scroll: The All list (~134 rows) scrolls smoothly with real UITableView physics: no blank rows or popping in during a fling, and it rubber-bands normally at the top. The large title collapses into the inline title properly.

requirements.note: Inset-grouped main screen titled 'Lists': Today and All, then 6 lists with open counts. Counts update correctly.
Open tasks, then a 'Completed (n)' row with a chevron that collapses and expands; the collapsed state persisted. Checkboxes complete and reopen tasks.

Adding works (title, notes, due-date switch with a compact date picker, priority segments). But tapping any task to edit it crashes the app straight to the Home Screen. Reproduced 4 times on new and seeded tasks in two lists, so editing is impossible.
Overdue rows are red with an icon and 'Overdue · Oct 21'. High priority is a red !!!, low a grey !.
Every row has a drag grip for direct reordering, and the order persisted. Swipe left shows Delete. The dragged row stays dimmed afterwards.
+ opens a New List sheet, Rename is in the list's ... menu, and swipe Delete on the main screen asks for confirmation in an alert.
After relaunch: the rename, the order, the added task, the deletions and the completions all survived.

bugs: Tapping any task to edit it crashes the app (reproduced in Errands and Garden, on seeded and new tasks).
After drag-reordering, the moved row stays faded (half opacity) until you leave the screen.
The New Task priority segmented control reports 'None' as selected to accessibility even after High is chosen visually.
tells: Every list icon is the same orange, so lists aren't told apart by colour as they are in Reminders.
Row metadata spacing is irregular: 'Nov 17  · Home', and notes sometimes run inline after the date and sometimes wrap below it. Rows sit tight against the separators.
At the largest text size the row metadata breaks into stray fragments ('· Errands X' alone on a line, '!' alone on a line) and the reorder grips disappear.
The swiped Delete pill runs to the screen edge and is clipped.
Rows are built from loose elements rather than real table cells (each row's checkbox reads as a switch).
B.scroll: The long All list scrolls and flings smoothly with no blank or popping rows, and it bounces normally at the top. The plain-style rows feel a bit cramped but the motion is native.

why: Both apps look like credible iOS to-do apps and cover most of the spec, but B crashes whenever you tap a task to edit it, so a core requirement doesn't work. A did everything without a single fault: native swipe actions, an inline calendar, colour-coded lists and consistent row layouts that hold up better at large text. B's direct drag grips are nice, but its stuck faded row and fragmented large-text layout add to the gap.
